redflag.t: Emergency symptoms with a very high reading: chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision or difficulty speaking.
redflag.q: * Symptoms: chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision or difficulty speaking.

redflag.t: Life-threatening symptoms listed by NICE: new confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, acute kidney injury.
redflag.q: life-threatening symptoms such as new onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, or acute kidney injury.

redflag.t: Call 999 for sudden chest pain or discomfort that does not go away (squeezing, pressure, burning, indigestion-like).
redflag.q: you get sudden pain or discomfort in your chest that does not go away – the pain can feel like squeezing or pressure inside your chest, burning or indigestion

redflag.t: Call 999 for pain spreading to an arm, neck, jaw, stomach or back.
redflag.q: you get pain that spreads to your left or right arm, or your neck, jaw, stomach or back

monitor.t: Take another reading a few minutes after the first to check it is accurate.
monitor.q: take another reading a few minutes after your first reading to check it's accurate

monitor.t: Sit in an upright chair with back support, feet flat, arm resting on a table.
monitor.q: sit on an upright chair with a back ... place your feet flat on the floor ... rest your arm on a table and relax your hand and arm

symptom.t: Rarely, high blood pressure can cause headaches.
symptom.q: Rarely, high blood pressure can cause symptoms such as: ... headaches

symptom.t: Rarely, blurred vision.
symptom.q: headaches ... blurred vision

symptom.t: Rarely, chest pain.
symptom.q: blurred vision ... chest pain ... But the only way to find out

risk.t: Age - more likely as you get older.
risk.q: your age – you're more likely to get high blood pressure as you get older

risk.t: Close relatives with high blood pressure.
risk.q: having close relatives with high blood pressure

risk.t: Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian background.
risk.q: your ethnicity – you're at higher risk if you have a Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian ethnic background

risk.t: Unhealthy diet, especially high in salt.
risk.q: having an unhealthy diet – especially a diet that's high in salt

prevention.t: Exercise regularly - at least 150 minutes a week.
prevention.q: exercise regularly – aim to do at least 150 minutes of exercise a week

prevention.t: Eat a healthy, balanced diet and lose weight if overweight.
prevention.q: have a healthy, balanced diet ... lose weight if you're overweight

prevention.t: Don't eat too much salt.
prevention.q: do not eat too much salt – avoid salty food or adding salt to your meals

prevention.t: Don't regularly drink more than 14 alcohol units a week.
prevention.q: do not drink too much alcohol – avoid drinking more than 14 alcohol units a week on a regular basis

prevention.t: Limit caffeine (coffee, tea, cola) and don't smoke.
prevention.q: do not drink too much caffeine – drinks high in caffeine include coffee, tea and cola ... do not smoke

summary.t: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense mental and physical symptoms, which can come on quickly for no clear reason.
summary.q: During a panic attack you get a rush of intense mental and physical symptoms. It can come on very quickly and for no apparent reason.

symptom.t: A racing heartbeat.
symptom.q: a racing heartbeat

symptom.t: Feeling faint, sweating, nausea.
symptom.q: a racing heartbeat ... feeling faint ... sweating ... nausea

symptom.t: Chest pain (can also be a heart attack sign - never assume).
symptom.q: nausea ... chest pain ... shortness of breath

differential.t: IMPORTANT: most panic symptoms can also be caused by other conditions, so it may not be a panic attack.
differential.q: Be aware that most of these symptoms can also be symptoms of other conditions or problems, so you may not always be experiencing a panic attack.

differential.t: Example: a racing heartbeat can be caused by very low blood pressure.
differential.q: For example, you may have a racing heartbeat if you have very low blood pressure.

redflag.t: Treat chest pain as a possible heart attack: call 999 for sudden chest pain or discomfort that does not go away.
redflag.q: you get sudden pain or discomfort in your chest that does not go away – the pain can feel like squeezing or pressure inside your chest, burning or indigestion

redflag.t: Call 999 if pain spreads to an arm, neck, jaw, stomach or back.
redflag.q: you get pain that spreads to your left or right arm, or your neck, jaw, stomach or back

redflag.t: Call 999 for chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness - these overlap with panic, so do not dismiss them.
redflag.q: you have chest pain and you feel sweaty, sick, light headed or short of breath

escalate.t: You could be having a heart attack - call 999 straight away.
escalate.q: You could be having a heart attack. Call 999 straight away as you need immediate treatment in hospital.

escalate.t: See a GP if you have been having panic disorder symptoms.
escalate.q: See a GP if you've been experiencing symptoms of panic disorder.

escalate.t: A GP may examine you to rule out other conditions causing the symptoms.
escalate.q: They may also carry out a physical examination to rule out other conditions that could be causing your symptoms.

action.t: During a panic attack: stay where you are if possible.
action.q: The next time you feel a panic attack coming on: ... stay where you are, if possible

action.t: Breathe slowly and deeply.
action.q: breathe slowly and deeply

action.t: Remind yourself the attack will pass.
action.q: remind yourself that the attack will pass

action.t: Focus on positive, peaceful, relaxing images.
action.q: focus on positive, peaceful and relaxing images

action.t: Remember it is not life-threatening (only once a heart attack or other emergency has been ruled out).
action.q: remember it's not life threatening

action.t: Breathing exercise: breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth.
action.q: Try breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth.

prevention.t: Learn breathing exercises for stress.
prevention.q: learn breathing exercises for stress to help ease symptoms

prevention.t: Do regular physical exercise to reduce stress.
prevention.q: do regular physical exercise to reduce stress and tension

prevention.t: Avoid sugary food and drinks, caffeine and alcohol, and stop smoking.
prevention.q: avoid sugary food and drinks, caffeine and alcohol, and stop smoking, as they can all make attacks worse

prevention.t: Try yoga or pilates to relax.
prevention.q: try activities like yoga and pilates, to help you relax

risk.t: A traumatic or very stressful life event, such as bereavement.
risk.q: a traumatic or very stressful life experience, such as bereavement

risk.t: A close family member with panic disorder.
risk.q: having a close family member with panic disorder

summary.t: An asthma attack is when symptoms are severe and breathing is difficult; it can be life-threatening.
summary.q: An asthma attack is when you have severe symptoms and it's difficult to breathe, which can be life-threatening.

symptom.t: Symptoms getting worse quickly (cough, breathlessness, wheezing, tight chest).
symptom.q: your symptoms are quickly getting worse (cough, breathlessness, wheezing or tight chest)

symptom.t: Reliever inhaler not helping as much as usual, or needed more often.
symptom.q: your reliever inhaler does not seem to be helping as much as usual, or you need it more often

symptom.t: Finding it difficult to walk or talk.
symptom.q: you're finding it difficult to walk or talk

action.t: Step 1: sit up straight and try to stay calm.
action.q: If you're having an asthma attack, sit up straight, to help your breathing. Try to stay calm.

action.t: Step 2 (blue reliever): 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until better, up to 10 puffs; shake between puffs, use a spacer if you have one.
action.q: If you have a blue reliever inhaler, take 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until you feel better, up to a maximum of 10 puffs.

action.t: Step 2 (AIR or MART inhaler): 1 puff every 1 to 3 minutes until better, up to 6 puffs.
action.q: If you have an AIR or MART inhaler (used for both preventing and treating symptoms), take 1 puff every 1 to 3 minutes until you feel better, up to a maximum of 6 puffs.

action.t: If your personal asthma action plan gives a different maximum, follow the plan.
action.q: If your personal asthma action plan has a different maximum dose for treating an asthma attack, follow the instructions in your plan.

action.t: If no better after 10 minutes and the ambulance hasn't arrived, use the inhaler again up to the same maximum.
action.q: If symptoms are no better after 10 minutes and an ambulance has not arrived, use an asthma inhaler again if you have one, taking up to the same maximum dose.

action.t: Helping someone: help them sit up in a comfortable position.
action.q: Help them to sit up in a comfortable position.

escalate.t: Call 999 if you feel worse at any point or don't feel better after 10 puffs (blue reliever).
escalate.q: If you feel worse at any point OR you don't feel better after 10 puffs, call 999 for an ambulance.

escalate.t: If still no better after repeating and the ambulance still hasn't come, call 999 again immediately.
escalate.q: If your symptoms are no better after repeating step 2, and the ambulance has still not arrived, contact 999 again immediately.

escalate.t: After recovering from an attack, see a GP within 2 days even if you feel better.
escalate.q: Even if you feel better, it's important to see a GP within 2 days to discuss your treatment and get advice to help prevent another asthma attack.

redflag.t: Call 999 if symptoms get worse at any time during an attack.
redflag.q: You or someone else is having an asthma attack and: ... start to feel worse at any time

redflag.t: Call 999 if not better after the maximum reliever dose.
redflag.q: do not feel better after taking the maximum dose using an asthma reliever inhaler

redflag.t: Call 999 if there is no asthma inhaler.
redflag.q: do not feel better after taking the maximum dose using an asthma reliever inhaler ... do not have an asthma inhaler

dont.t: Do not wait to see if you get better on your own if you have no reliever and are struggling to breathe.
dont.q: Do not wait to see if you get better on your own. An asthma attack makes it hard to breathe, which is a medical emergency.

dont.t: Do not drive yourself to A&E.
dont.q: do not have an asthma inhaler ... Do not drive yourself to A&E.

dont.t: Don't take other medicines without checking - aspirin, ibuprofen and beta blockers can trigger asthma in some people.
dont.q: do not take medicines for other conditions without checking with a pharmacist or doctor – some medicines such as aspirin, ibuprofen and beta blockers can trigger asthma symptoms in some people

prevention.t: Always carry your inhaler.
prevention.q: always have your inhaler with you

prevention.t: Avoid triggers such as air pollution, smoke, pollen or animals.
prevention.q: try to avoid things that trigger your asthma symptoms, such as air pollution, smoke, pollen or animals

prevention.t: Exercise regularly (ask how to do it safely if exercise is a trigger).
prevention.q: exercise regularly – get advice from your doctor or nurse about exercising safely if exercise triggers your asthma symptoms

prevention.t: Keep a healthy weight and have vaccinations such as flu.
prevention.q: keep to a healthy weight ... have vaccinations such as the flu vaccine

prevention.t: Do not smoke.
prevention.q: do not smoke – get help to quit smoking if you need it

risk.t: Triggers include exercise, air pollution, cold air, and allergens such as pollen, dust, mould or animals.
risk.q: Symptoms can be triggered by different things including exercise, high levels of air pollution, cold air, or contact with something you're allergic to, such as pollen, dust, mould or animals.

risk.t: Having allergies such as eczema, hay fever or food allergies.
risk.q: you have allergies such as eczema, hay fever or food allergies

meds.name: Blue reliever inhaler (e.g. salbutamol) - prescribed
meds.purpose: Quick relief of asthma symptoms during an attack.
meds.q: If you have a blue reliever inhaler, take 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until you feel better, up to a maximum of 10 puffs. Shake the inhaler between each puff and use a spacer with the inhaler if you have one.

cautions.t: If the personal asthma action plan gives a different maximum, follow the plan.
cautions.q: If your personal asthma action plan has a different maximum dose for treating an asthma attack, follow the instructions in your plan.

cautions.t: Call 999 if not better after 10 puffs or worse at any point.
cautions.q: If you feel worse at any point OR you don't feel better after 10 puffs, call 999 for an ambulance.

cautions.t: A blue reliever should not be prescribed on its own (it comes with a preventer).
cautions.q: you should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own

summary.t: Sepsis is a serious, life-threatening reaction to an infection. It develops very quickly and needs urgent hospital treatment.
summary.q: Sepsis is a serious reaction to an infection that can be life-threatening. It develops very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

symptom.t: Confusion or slurred speech.
symptom.q: Common symptoms of sepsis in adults include: ... confusion or slurred speech

symptom.t: Uncontrollable shivering.
symptom.q: uncontrollable shivering

symptom.t: Muscle pain.
symptom.q: Common symptoms of sepsis in adults include: ... muscle pain

redflag.t: Call 999 if an adult is breathing very fast.
redflag.q: An adult or child aged 5 years or over: ... is breathing very fast

redflag.t: Call 999 if confused, slurred speech or not making sense.
redflag.q: is confused, has slurred speech, or is not making sense

redflag.t: Call 999 if skin is blue, pale or blotchy.
redflag.q: An adult or child aged 5 years or over: ... has blue, pale or blotchy skin

redflag.t: Call 999 if very high or very low temperature, feels hot or cold, or shivery.
redflag.q: has a very high or very low temperature, feels hot or cold to the touch, or is shivery

escalate.t: Trust your instincts: not every symptom has to be present - get immediate help if something seems seriously wrong.
escalate.q: A child or adult with sepsis might not have every symptom listed. Get immediate medical help if you or your child are unwell and you think there's something seriously wrong.

escalate.t: Call NHS 111 if you had sepsis in the last 12 months and now have signs of infection.
escalate.q: you or your child have had sepsis in the past 12 months and have symptoms of an infection, such as a very high temperature, or feeling hot, cold or shivery

monitor.t: Sepsis can be harder to notice in people with dementia or who have difficulty communicating.
monitor.q: Symptoms of sepsis can be more difficult to notice in some people, such as: ... people with dementia ... people with a learning disability ... people who have difficulty communicating

monitor.t: Recovery: keep a diary of sleep, exercise and symptoms.
monitor.q: keep a diary to track your progress – you can record things like your sleep, exercise and any symptoms you have

risk.t: Any infection can lead to sepsis; chest infections and urine infections (UTIs) are common causes.
risk.q: Any type of infection can lead to sepsis, but bacterial infections are the most common cause, including: ... chest infections (pneumonia) ... urinary tract infections (UTIs)

risk.t: Higher risk if over 75.
risk.q: you're over 75 years

risk.t: Higher risk with a weakened immune system (e.g. chemotherapy, steroids, immunosuppressants).
risk.q: your immune system is weakened because you have a condition like HIV or sickle cell disease, you're having chemotherapy, or you're taking corticosteroids or immunosuppressants

risk.t: Higher risk with a burn, cut, wound or skin infection.
risk.q: you have a burn, cut or wound, or a skin infection like cellulitis

prevention.t: Recovery: be patient and do not rush.
prevention.q: be patient and give yourself plenty of time – try not to rush your recovery

prevention.t: Recovery: get 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
prevention.q: try to get enough sleep – adults usually need 7 to 9 hours' sleep each night

prevention.t: Recovery: eat a balanced diet; smaller, more frequent meals if appetite is low.
prevention.q: eat a healthy, balanced diet – if you have a reduced appetite, eating smaller meals more frequently may help

prevention.t: Recovery: exercise regularly, starting slowly.
prevention.q: exercise regularly, but start slowly and build up gradually

summary.t: A high temperature (fever) is usually a sign of infection and often gets better on its own with home care.
summary.q: A high temperature (fever) is usually a symptom of an infection. It often improves on its own and there are things you can do at home to help treat it.

symptom.t: Chest or back feels hotter than usual.
symptom.q: your chest or back feels hotter than usual

symptom.t: Feeling hot or cold, shivery (chills), sweating, or warm red skin.
symptom.q: feeling hot or cold, feeling shivery (chills), sweating, or your skin being warm and red

symptom.t: Flu: sudden high temperature, aching body, exhaustion, dry cough, sore throat, headache.
symptom.q: Flu symptoms come on very quickly and can include: ... a sudden high temperature ... an aching body ... feeling tired or exhausted ... a dry cough ... a sore throat ... a headache

monitor.t: You may have a fever even if the thermometer reads below 38C if you feel hot, cold or shivery.
monitor.q: If you feel hot, cold or shivery, you may have a high temperature even if a thermometer says your temperature is below 38C.

monitor.t: Digital thermometer: put the tip under the tongue towards the back of the mouth.
monitor.q: Put the tip under your tongue, towards the back of your mouth.

dont.t: Do not rely on forehead strips - they are not accurate.
dont.q: forehead strips because they're not accurate

differential.t: Flu comes on within hours and makes you too unwell to carry on; a cold comes on gradually and is milder.
differential.q: Cold and flu symptoms are similar, but flu tends to be more severe.

action.t: Get lots of rest.
action.q: get lots of rest

action.t: Drink plenty of fluids (water is best) so pee is light yellow and clear.
action.q: drink plenty of fluids (water is best) to avoid dehydration – drink enough so your pee is light yellow and clear

action.t: Stay away from other people until the fever has gone.
action.q: Try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people until you do not have a high temperature.

action.t: Flu: rest and sleep.
action.q: rest and sleep

escalate.t: Get an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the fever is not improving or is getting worse with home treatment.
escalate.q: a high temperature and you've been treating it at home but it's not getting better or is getting worse

escalate.t: Flu: get urgent advice if 65 or over.
escalate.q: You or your child have symptoms of flu and: ... you're 65 or over

escalate.t: Flu: get urgent advice with a long-term condition (diabetes, heart, lung, kidney, brain conditions).
escalate.q: you have a long-term medical condition – for example, diabetes or a condition that affects your heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, brain or nerves

redflag.t: Call 999 for sudden chest pain.
redflag.q: you get sudden chest pain

redflag.t: Call 999 for severe difficulty breathing (gasping, choking, cannot speak).
redflag.q: you have severe difficulty breathing – you're gasping, choking or not able to get words out

redflag.t: Call 999 if coughing up blood.
redflag.q: you start coughing up blood

prevention.t: Wash hands often with warm water and soap.
prevention.q: wash your hands often with warm water and soap

prevention.t: Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow; bin tissues quickly.
prevention.q: cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when you cough or sneeze

prevention.t: Flu is most infectious in the first 5 days.
prevention.q: You're more likely to give it to others in the first 5 days after getting infected.

prevention.t: The flu vaccine helps protect against flu.
prevention.q: The flu vaccine helps protect against flu.

meds.name: Paracetamol or ibuprofen
meds.purpose: Ease discomfort from a high temperature.
meds.q: take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel uncomfortable

cautions.t: Do not give aspirin to children under 16.
cautions.q: do not give aspirin to children under the age of 16

cautions.t: Do not take paracetamol together with flu remedies that also contain paracetamol.
cautions.q: Do not take paracetamol and flu remedies that contain paracetamol at the same time as it's easy to take more than the recommended dose.

cautions.t: The NHS adult paracetamol advice is for people aged 18 or over; children have separate advice.
cautions.q: This information is for adults aged 18 or over.

cautions.t: Adult dose for 500mg tablets: 1 or 2 tablets, at least 4 hours apart, no more than 8 tablets in 24 hours.
cautions.q: For 500mg tablets and capsules: ... one dose is 1 or 2 tablets or capsules ... leave at least 4 hours between each dose ... do not take more than 8 tablets or capsules in 24 hours

cautions.t: People who weigh less than 50kg may need a lower dose.
cautions.q: if you weigh less than 50kg, you may need to take a lower dose

cautions.t: Do not use paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor says so.
cautions.q: Do not take or use paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to.

cautions.t: Do not take it together with other products that also contain paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies.
cautions.q: You should also avoid taking paracetamol at the same time as other medicines containing paracetamol, for example, cold and flu remedies.

cautions.t: May not be suitable if you have had an allergic reaction to paracetamol.
cautions.q: had an allergic reaction to paracetamol before

cautions.t: May not be suitable if you have a kidney or liver condition.
cautions.q: you have a kidney or liver condition

meds.name: Paracetamol or ibuprofen (flu)
meds.purpose: Lower temperature and ease aches and pains from flu.
meds.q: take paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower your temperature and treat aches and pains

cautions.t: Do not give aspirin to children under 16.
cautions.q: do not give aspirin to children under the age of 16

cautions.t: Do not take paracetamol together with flu remedies that also contain paracetamol.
cautions.q: Do not take paracetamol and flu remedies that contain paracetamol at the same time as it's easy to take more than the recommended dose.

cautions.t: The NHS adult paracetamol advice is for people aged 18 or over; children have separate advice.
cautions.q: This information is for adults aged 18 or over.

cautions.t: Adult dose for 500mg tablets: 1 or 2 tablets, at least 4 hours apart, no more than 8 tablets in 24 hours.
cautions.q: For 500mg tablets and capsules: ... one dose is 1 or 2 tablets or capsules ... leave at least 4 hours between each dose ... do not take more than 8 tablets or capsules in 24 hours

cautions.t: People who weigh less than 50kg may need a lower dose.
cautions.q: if you weigh less than 50kg, you may need to take a lower dose

cautions.t: Do not use paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor says so.
cautions.q: Do not take or use paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to.

cautions.t: Do not take it together with other products that also contain paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies.
cautions.q: You should also avoid taking paracetamol at the same time as other medicines containing paracetamol, for example, cold and flu remedies.

cautions.t: May not be suitable if you have had an allergic reaction to paracetamol.
cautions.q: had an allergic reaction to paracetamol before

cautions.t: May not be suitable if you have a kidney or liver condition.
cautions.q: you have a kidney or liver condition

summary.t: Heat exhaustion usually is not an emergency if the person cools down within 30 minutes; heatstroke is an emergency.
summary.q: Heat exhaustion does not usually need emergency medical help if you can cool down within 30 minutes. If it turns into heatstroke, it needs to be treated as an emergency.

symptom.t: Tiredness.
symptom.q: The symptoms of heat exhaustion include: ... tiredness

symptom.t: Dizziness.
symptom.q: The symptoms of heat exhaustion include: ... dizziness

symptom.t: Headache.
symptom.q: The symptoms of heat exhaustion include: ... headache

redflag.t: Heatstroke is a medical emergency.
redflag.q: Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Get immediate medical help if someone has the symptoms of heatstroke.

redflag.t: Call 999 if still unwell after 30 minutes of resting, cooling and drinking.
redflag.q: still being unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled and drinking fluids

redflag.t: Call 999 for a very high temperature.
redflag.q: You or someone else have signs of heatstroke, including: ... a very high temperature

redflag.t: Call 999 for hot skin that is not sweating.
redflag.q: hot skin that's not sweating and might look red

action.t: Step 1: Move them to a cool place.
action.q: Move them to a cool place.

action.t: Step 2: Remove unnecessary clothing like a jacket or socks.
action.q: Remove all unnecessary clothing like a jacket or socks.

action.t: Step 3: Give plenty of water (or a sports drink / oral rehydration drink).
action.q: Give them plenty of water to drink

action.t: Step 4: Cool the skin with cool water and fanning; wrapped cold packs under armpits or on the neck.
action.q: Cool their skin – spray or sponge them with cool water and fan them. Cold packs, wrapped in a cloth and put under the armpits or on the neck are good too.

action.t: Stay with them until they are better.
action.q: Stay with them until they're better.

action.t: Heatstroke while waiting for help: wrap in a cool wet sheet, fan, or sponge with cold water.
action.q: Wrap the person in a cool, wet sheet, or fan them or sponge them down with cold water while you wait for help to arrive.

monitor.t: They should cool down and feel better within 30 minutes.
monitor.q: They should start to cool down and feel better within 30 minutes.

escalate.t: Get help from NHS 111 if heat exhaustion is hard to treat or you need advice.
escalate.q: you or someone else have symptoms of heat exhaustion that you're struggling to treat or you need advice about

risk.t: High risk during hot weather or exercise.
risk.q: There's a high risk of heat exhaustion or heatstroke during hot weather or exercise.

risk.t: Older people and people with long-term conditions such as diabetes or heart problems are more at risk.
risk.q: Check on children, older people and people with long-term health conditions, such as diabetes or heart problems, as they're more at risk of heat exhaustion or heatstroke.

prevention.t: Drink more cold drinks, especially when active.
prevention.q: drink more cold drinks, especially if you're active or exercising

prevention.t: Wear light-coloured, loose clothing.
prevention.q: wear light-coloured, loose clothing

prevention.t: Avoid the sun between 11am and 3pm.
prevention.q: avoid the sun between 11am and 3pm

prevention.t: Avoid too much alcohol and extreme exercise.
prevention.q: avoid drinking too much alcohol ... avoid extreme exercise

prevention.t: Indoors on a hot day: close curtains, close windows if hotter outside, turn off hot electrical equipment.
prevention.q: if you're inside on a very hot day, close curtains, and close windows if it's hotter outside than in your home, and turn off electrical equipment and lights that get hot

meds.name: Oral rehydration powder or isotonic sports drink
meds.purpose: Replace salt lost through sweating while cooling down.
meds.q: you can also give them an isotonic sports drink or oral rehydration powder that you mix with water, which will help replace salt lost through sweating

summary.t: Anyone can fall, but it is more likely when older or with mobility problems.
summary.q: Anyone can have a fall, but it's more likely if you're older or have mobility problems.

action.t: Step 1: Stay calm; take a couple of minutes to check for pain or injury before trying to get up.
action.q: If you fall, try to stay calm. Take a couple of minutes to check for any pain or injuries and see if you think you can get up.

action.t: Getting up 1: Take your time - do not get up too quickly.
action.q: Take your time – do not get up too quickly.

action.t: Getting up 2: Roll onto your side, then push up onto hands and knees.
action.q: Roll onto your side, then use your arms to push yourself onto your hands and knees.

action.t: Getting up 3: Crawl to something stable (heavy furniture) to hold.
action.q: Look for something stable to hold, such as a heavy piece of furniture or a bath or sink. Crawl to it if it's out of reach.

action.t: Getting up 4: Put one foot flat on the floor and stand slowly while holding on.
action.q: Put one foot flat on the floor. Stand up slowly, holding onto something stable to help you.

action.t: Getting up 5: Sit down and rest.
action.q: Sit down and rest while you recover.

redflag.t: Call 999 if the person may have hurt their head, back, neck or hip.
redflag.q: You or someone else has fallen and: ... may have injured the head, back, neck or hip

redflag.t: Call 999 if they cannot get up.
redflag.q: You or someone else has fallen and: ... cannot get up

redflag.t: Call 999 for severe hip pain after a fall.
redflag.q: you have severe hip pain after a fall or injury

redflag.t: Call 999 if unable to walk or put weight on the leg.
redflag.q: you're unable to walk or put weight on your leg

dont.t: Helping someone: keep them comfortable and warm; do not try to lift them yourself.
dont.q: If someone else has fallen, keep them comfortable and warm. Carefully help them get up if they can, but do not try to lift them yourself.

dont.t: Do not eat or drink in case surgery is needed.
dont.q: avoid eating or drinking in case you need surgery

dont.t: Do not try to use the injured arm or wrist.
dont.q: do not try to use the affected arm or wrist

escalate.t: NHS 111 if fallen and may be in pain, injured or unwell.
escalate.q: you or someone else has fallen and may be in pain, injured or unwell

escalate.t: See a GP after any fall or if worried about balance.

summary.t: Dehydration means the body loses more fluid than it takes in; untreated it can become serious.
summary.q: Dehydration means your body loses more fluids than you take in. If it's not treated, it can get worse and become a serious problem.

summary.t: Staying hydrated is critical: dehydration harms decision-making, concentration and body function.
summary.q: Being well hydrated during operations is absolutely critical as dehydration can result in decrements in decision-making, concentration, and physiology of the crew.

risk.t: Babies, children and older adults are more at risk.
risk.q: Babies, children and older adults are more at risk of dehydration.

risk.t: Diabetes, vomiting or diarrhoea, heat, alcohol, heavy sweating, fever.
risk.q: have diabetes ... have been sick or have diarrhoea ... have been in the sun, or a hot environment, too long (heatstroke) ... have drunk too much alcohol ... sweat a lot after exercising ... have a high temperature

risk.t: Water tablets (diuretics) and relying on others for drinks raise the risk.
risk.q: take medicines that make you pee more (diuretics) ... rely on other people to get you drinks

escalate.q: you feel dizzy when you stand up and it does not go away

escalate.q: you have dark yellow pee or you're peeing less than normal

redflag.t: Call 999 if dehydrated with blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue.
redflag.q: You or somebody else has signs of dehydration and: ... blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue

redflag.t: Call 999 if skin feels cold.
redflag.q: skin that feels cold

redflag.t: Call 999 if difficulty breathing or lots of quick breaths.
redflag.q: difficulty breathing, or is taking lots of quick breaths

redflag.t: Call 999 if confused.
redflag.q: You or somebody else has signs of dehydration and: ... are confused

prevention.t: Drink more when sick, sweating from heat or exercise, or with diarrhoea.
prevention.q: Drink more when there's a higher risk of dehydrating. For example, if you're being sick, sweating due to hot weather or exercise, or you have diarrhoea.

prevention.t: Older adults should get plenty of fluids.
prevention.q: Children under the age of 5 and older adults should get plenty of fluids as they have an increased risk of dehydration.

prevention.t: Carers: make sure they drink at mealtimes and always have drinks within reach.

prevention.t: ESA doctor at Concordia keeps a water bottle close at night because of the dry air.
prevention.q: I often wake up with a dry mouth so I keep a bottle of water close at all times.

monitor.t: Drink enough so your pee is pale.

monitor.t: People you care for may not notice how little they drink.

summary.t: Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C. It is an emergency that needs hospital treatment.
summary.q: Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C (normal body temperature is around 37C). It's a medical emergency that needs to be treated in hospital.

symptom.t: Shivering.
symptom.q: Symptoms of hypothermia include: ... shivering

symptom.t: Pale, cold, dry skin; skin and lips may turn blue or grey.
symptom.q: pale, cold and dry skin – skin and lips may turn blue or grey

symptom.t: Slurred speech.
symptom.q: slurred speech

redflag.t: Late (severe) signs: shivering stops, skin turns blue, pupils widen, pulse and breathing slow, and the person may pass out.
redflag.q: Late symptoms ... No shivering ... Blue skin ... Dilated pupils ... Slowed pulse and breathing ... Loss of consciousness

redflag.t: Severe hypothermia: the person may be unconscious and seem to have no pulse or breathing - get emergency help immediately.
redflag.q: A person with severe hypothermia may be unconscious and may not seem to have a pulse or to be breathing.

escalate.t: Call 999 (emergency) or go to A&E if you think someone has hypothermia.
escalate.q: Go to A&E or call 999 if: ... you think you or your child have hypothermia

escalate.t: If body temperature is below 95F (35C), get medical attention immediately.
escalate.q: If a person's temperature is below 95 degrees get medical attention immediately.

action.t: Step 1: Move the person indoors or to shelter as quickly as possible.
action.q: move the person indoors or somewhere sheltered as quickly as possible

action.t: Step 2: Remove wet clothing and wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel, covering the head.
action.q: remove any wet clothing, wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel, making sure their head is covered

action.t: Step 3: If they are fully awake, give a warm non-alcoholic drink and sugary food such as chocolate.
action.q: give them a warm non-alcoholic drink and some sugary food like chocolate if they're fully awake

action.t: Step 4: Keep them awake by talking to them until help arrives.
action.q: keep them awake by talking to them until help arrives

action.t: Step 5: Make sure someone stays with them.
action.q: make sure you or someone else stays with them

action.t: If help is delayed, warm the centre of the body first (chest, neck, head, groin), e.g. with an electric blanket or skin-to-skin contact under dry layers.
action.q: Warm the center of the person's body-chest, neck, head, and groin-using an electric blanket, if available. You can also use skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers of blankets, clothing, towels, or sheets.

dont.t: Do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp to warm them.
dont.q: do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp to warm them up

dont.t: Do not rub their arms, legs, feet or hands.
dont.q: do not rub their arms, legs, feet or hands

dont.t: Do not give them alcohol.
dont.q: do not give them alcohol to drink

monitor.t: Keep an eye on your own condition and on your teammates when working in the cold.
monitor.q: Monitor your physical condition and that of your coworkers.

risk.t: Older people living alone in a cold home are particularly at risk.
risk.q: live in a cold house – older people living alone are particularly at risk

risk.t: Staying out in the cold too long, falling into cold water or having wet clothes.
risk.q: stay out in the cold too long ... fall into cold water ... have wet clothes and get cold

risk.t: Older adults without enough food, clothing or heating.
risk.q: Older adults with inadequate food, clothing, or heating

risk.t: Drinking alcohol or using drugs raises the risk.
risk.q: People who drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

prevention.t: Wear several loose layers.
prevention.q: Wear several layers of loose clothing for better insulation.

prevention.t: Protect ears, face, hands and feet; wear a hat.
prevention.q: Make sure to protect the ears, face, hands, and feet.

prevention.t: Go to warm places during breaks.
prevention.q: Move into warm locations during breaks.

prevention.t: Carry spare socks, gloves, hat, jacket, clothes and blankets.
prevention.q: Carry extra socks, gloves, hat, jacket, clothes, and blankets.

prevention.t: Keep a thermometer and chemical hot packs in the first aid kit.
prevention.q: Include a thermometer and chemical hot packs in your first aid kit.

summary.t: Frostbite is when skin freezes in very cold temperatures. The skin needs warming as soon as possible and medical help.
summary.q: Frostbite happens when your skin freezes after being in very cold temperatures. The skin needs to be warmed as soon as possible.

symptom.t: Early: skin is cold and firm, numb, or stinging/burning.
symptom.q: At first, your skin may be: ... cold and firm ... numb, or you may feel a stinging or burning sensation

symptom.t: Early: skin is painful, throbbing or aching.
symptom.q: painful, throb or ache

symptom.t: Early: skin looks red or pale.
symptom.q: red or pale (redness may be harder to see on black or brown skin)

redflag.t: Worse: hard, frozen skin that is white, blue or blotchy.
redflag.q: hard, frozen skin that can be white, blue or blotchy

redflag.t: Worse: swelling and loss of feeling in the area.
redflag.q: swelling and loss of feeling in the affected area

redflag.t: Worse: blisters filled with blood or clear/milky fluid.
redflag.q: blisters filled with blood or clear or milky fluid

redflag.t: Severe: skin turns black and hard as it starts to die.
redflag.q: the skin turns black and hard as it starts to die

escalate.t: Call 999 / go to A&E after cold exposure if there is hard frozen skin, swelling with loss of feeling, or blisters.
escalate.q: You've been exposed to very cold temperatures and: ... have hard, frozen skin ... have swelling and loss of feeling in the affected area ... have blisters filled with blood or a clear or milky fluid

escalate.t: Get medical help for any suspected frostbite.
escalate.q: Get medical help if you think you or someone else has frostbite.

escalate.t: Frostbite should always be checked by a health professional.
escalate.q: Frostbite should be checked by a health care provider.

differential.t: Check for hypothermia too - it is more serious and needs emergency care.
differential.q: Check to see if the person is also showing signs of hypothermia. Hypothermia is a more serious condition and requires emergency medical care.

differential.t: Shivering a lot or struggling to stay awake may mean hypothermia.
differential.q: If the person is shivering a lot or struggling to stay awake, they may have hypothermia (very low body temperature).

action.t: Step 1: Go indoors or to shelter as quickly as possible.
action.q: go indoors or somewhere sheltered as quickly as possible

action.t: Step 2: Remove gloves, rings, boots and jewellery from the affected area.
action.q: remove clothing and jewellery, such as gloves, rings and boots from the affected area

action.t: Step 3: Wrap up in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel.
action.q: wrap yourself in something warm like a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel

action.t: Step 4: Warm affected hands in your armpits.
action.q: put your hands in your armpits (if your hands are affected)

action.t: Helper: hold the affected part in your lap and gently warm it with your hands.
action.q: if you're with someone who has frostbite, place the affected body part in your lap and gently warm it with your hands

action.t: Step 5: Put the part in warm (not hot) water, dry it, and apply a light dressing such as gauze.
action.q: place the affected body part in warm (not hot) water, dry it and put on a light dressing, such as a gauze bandage, if you have one

dont.t: Do not thaw a frostbitten area if it might refreeze - refreezing makes damage worse. Rewarming may be better delayed until a warm, safe place is reached.
dont.q: If protection from refreezing cannot be guaranteed, it may be better to delay the initial rewarming process until a warm, safe location is reached.

dont.t: Do not thaw a frostbitten area if it cannot be kept thawed - refreezing makes tissue damage worse.
dont.q: In case of frostbite, do not: ... Thaw out a frostbitten area if it cannot be kept thawed. Refreezing may make tissue damage even worse.

dont.t: Do not rub the affected area.
dont.q: do not rub the affected area

monitor.t: Frozen skin is numb, so the person may not notice - teammates should check each other.
monitor.q: A person who has frostbite may not know they have it until someone else points it out because the frozen parts of their body are numb.

risk.t: Frostbite can happen when skin is exposed to 0C (32F) or below.
risk.q: You can get frostbite if your skin is exposed to temperatures of 0C (32F) or below.

risk.t: The colder it is and the longer the exposure, the worse it gets.
risk.q: Frostbite gets worse the colder it is and the longer you're exposed to the cold.

risk.t: Poor blood circulation raises the risk.
risk.q: You may have a greater chance of developing frostbite if you: ... Have poor blood circulation

risk.t: Smoking, diabetes, beta-blocker medicines and Raynaud phenomenon raise the risk.
risk.q: Take medicines called beta-blockers ... Have poor blood supply to the legs (peripheral vascular disease) ... Smoke or use tobacco ... Have diabetes ... Have Raynaud phenomenon

prevention.q: several loose layers of clothing with a waterproof outer layer

prevention.t: Wear a hat and scarf to protect head, neck and face.
prevention.q: a hat and scarf to protect your head, neck and face

prevention.t: Wear gloves or mittens.
prevention.q: gloves or mittens to protect your hands and fingers

prevention.t: Wear thick socks and boots.

summary.t: Altitude sickness can happen at high altitude. It usually gets better in a few days with rest but can sometimes be life-threatening.
summary.q: Altitude sickness can happen when you're at a high altitude. It usually gets better in a few days with rest, but it can sometimes be life-threatening and need treatment.

risk.t: High altitude usually means above 2,500 metres.
risk.q: You can get altitude sickness if you're in a place that is at a high altitude (usually more than 2,500 metres above sea level).

risk.t: Concordia station sits at about 3,200 m above sea level.
risk.q: At 3200 metres above sea level, with winter temperatures plummeting to –80 °C and four months of total darkness each year, life here is harsher than almost anywhere else on Earth.

risk.t: Concordia is on the Dome C plateau about 3,200 m above sea level.
risk.q: located on Dome C, a plateau some 3200 m above sea level

symptom.q: The main symptoms include: ... a headache

symptom.t: Loss of appetite.
