cautions.t: May not be suitable if you are dependent on alcohol or binge drink.
cautions.q: you're dependent on alcohol or binge drink (drink heavily over a short period of time)

cautions.t: May not mix well with blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin.
cautions.q: medicines to help prevent blood clots, such as warfarin

meds.name: Anti-sickness medicine
meds.purpose: Ease nausea/vomiting from altitude sickness.
meds.q: you can take anti-sickness medicine or painkillers such as ibuprofen or paracetamol to ease symptoms

cautions.t: Some anti-sickness medicines (metoclopramide, domperidone) may not mix well with paracetamol.
cautions.q: medicines that stop you being sick, including metoclopramide and domperidone

summary.t: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas made by fires and fuel-burning appliances; breathing it in can make you seriously ill.
summary.q: Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas that can make you seriously ill if you breathe it in. Carbon monoxide can be made by fires and appliances that burn gas, wood, oil or coal.

symptom.t: Headache.
symptom.q: Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include: ... a headache

symptom.t: Dizziness.
symptom.q: Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include: ... dizziness

symptom.t: Feeling or being sick.
symptom.q: feeling sick or being sick

monitor.t: Key clue: symptoms come and go, get worse in a particular room or building and better when you leave or go outside.
monitor.q: The symptoms may come and go. They may get worse when you spend time in an affected room or building and get better when you leave or go outside.

differential.t: CO symptoms are often described as "flu-like".
differential.q: The most common symptoms of CO poisoning are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. CO symptoms are often described as "flu-like."

redflag.t: People who are asleep or drunk can die from CO before they notice symptoms.
redflag.q: People who are sleeping, drunk, or under the influence of other substances can die from CO poisoning before they have symptoms.

redflag.t: Call 999 if exposed to CO and finding it hard to breathe.
redflag.q: You think you or someone else has been exposed to carbon monoxide and: ... are finding it hard to breathe

redflag.t: Call 999 if suddenly confused.
redflag.q: have suddenly become confused

redflag.t: Call 999 if they have lost consciousness.
redflag.q: have lost consciousness

action.t: Step 1: Stop using the appliance you suspect (boiler, cooker, heater) if you can.
action.q: stop using appliances you think might be making carbon monoxide (such as a boiler, cooker or heater) if you can

action.t: Step 2: Go outside into fresh air.
action.q: If you think you might have carbon monoxide poisoning: ... go outside

action.t: Step 3: Get medical advice as soon as possible; do not go back in until advised.
action.q: get medical advice as soon as possible – do not go back into the affected building until you have got advice

escalate.t: Call NHS 111 if you think you might have CO poisoning symptoms.
escalate.q: Call NHS 111 if: ... you think you might have symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning

risk.t: Faulty, badly installed or poorly maintained heating and cooking appliances can make CO.
risk.q: Common household appliances used for heating and cooking can produce carbon monoxide if they are not installed properly, are faulty or are poorly maintained.

risk.t: Sources include gas or paraffin heaters, fires and portable generators.
risk.q: gas or paraffin heaters ... wood, gas and coal fires ... portable generators

risk.t: Barbecues or camping stoves inside, or engines running in enclosed spaces, can build up CO.
risk.q: Using barbecues or camping stoves inside, and turning on vehicle or lawn mower engines in an enclosed space (such as a garage) can also cause a build-up of carbon monoxide.

risk.t: Older people and those with heart disease, anaemia or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.
risk.q: Infants, the elderly, and people with chronic heart disease, anemia, or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.

prevention.t: Fit a loud CO alarm in every room with a fuel-burning appliance.
prevention.q: get a carbon monoxide alarm that makes a loud sound if there's carbon monoxide present – get 1 for each room of your home containing appliances that burn gas, oil, coal or wood

prevention.t: Put battery or battery-backup CO detectors near every sleeping area.
prevention.q: Install battery-operated or battery back-up CO detectors near every sleeping area in your home.

prevention.t: Have boilers, heaters and cookers serviced regularly by a qualified engineer.
prevention.q: make sure boilers, heaters and cookers are serviced regularly by a qualified and registered engineer

prevention.t: Keep rooms ventilated and chimneys/flues clean.
prevention.q: keep rooms well ventilated, and make sure chimneys and flues are clean and well maintained

dont.t: Never use a barbecue or camping stove indoors or in a tent.
dont.q: do not use a barbecue or camping stove indoors or inside a tent

dont.t: Never leave vehicles or engines running in enclosed spaces.
dont.q: do not leave vehicles or other engines on in enclosed spaces (such as a garage)

dont.t: Never run a generator indoors, even with doors and windows open.
dont.q: Never use a generator inside your home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.

summary.t: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a type of depression that usually happens in winter.
summary.q: Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is a type of depression that usually happens in the winter.

symptom.t: Low mood.
symptom.q: Symptoms of seasonal affective disorder include: ... low mood

symptom.t: Losing interest in things you usually enjoy.
symptom.q: a lack of interest in things you usually enjoy

symptom.t: Feeling guilty, hopeless or worthless.
symptom.q: feeling guilty, hopeless or worthless

redflag.t: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm - get urgent help.
redflag.q: thoughts of suicide or self-harm

redflag.t: Call 999 if someone's life is at risk, e.g. serious self-injury or overdose.
redflag.q: someone's life is at risk – for example, they have seriously injured themselves or taken an overdose

redflag.t: Call 999 if you do not feel you can keep yourself or someone else safe.
redflag.q: you do not feel you can keep yourself or someone else safe

escalate.t: See a GP (doctor) if you think you might have SAD.
escalate.q: See a GP if: ... you think you might have seasonal affective disorder (SAD)

escalate.t: See a GP if diagnosed with SAD and treatment is not helping.
escalate.q: you've been diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder and treatment is not helping

escalate.t: Urgent help is available for a mental health crisis.
escalate.q: Support is available if you or someone you know is having a mental health crisis or emergency, no matter what you're going through.

risk.t: SAD is thought to be linked to less daylight in winter.
risk.q: it's thought to be linked to reduced levels of daylight in winter

risk.t: This may change brain chemicals (melatonin, serotonin) that affect mood and sleep patterns.
risk.q: This may cause changes to brain chemicals like melatonin and serotonin that affect your mood and your sleeping patterns (circadian rhythm).

risk.t: At Concordia the Sun does not rise in winter (polar night), affecting body clock and mood.
risk.q: The Sun does not rise above the horizon in the winter during the polar night, and does not set in the summer, impacting circadian rhythm and mood.

risk.t: Concordia has about four months of total darkness each year.
risk.q: four months of total darkness each year

action.t: Get as much natural daylight as you can; go outside in the daytime every day.
action.q: get as much natural daylight as you can – try to go outside in the daytime every day

action.t: Get regular exercise.
action.q: get regular exercise

action.t: Stay in contact with friends and family.
action.q: stay in contact with friends and family

action.t: Keep up your usual activities.
action.q: keep up with your usual activities

action.t: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day.
action.q: try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day

dont.t: Do not drink too much alcohol or use illegal drugs.
dont.q: do not drink too much alcohol or use illegal drugs

dont.t: Avoid phones and other screens right before bed.
dont.q: do not use electronic devices, such as smartphones, right before going to bed

dont.t: Speak to a doctor before light therapy - it may not suit some eye conditions or light-sensitising medicines.
dont.q: Speak to a GP before trying light therapy. It might not be suitable if you have certain eye conditions or are taking some medicines that increase your sensitivity to light.

prevention.t: ESA doctor at Concordia: keep regular sleep and wake times to keep the body clock working when there is no sunlight.
prevention.q: I try to wake up and go to bed at regular times to promote sleep and maintain a functioning biological clock (without sunlight it relies even more on social clues)

prevention.t: ESA doctor at Concordia: limit bright screens in the evening; keep a daylight lamp for the darkest months.
prevention.q: while I restrict myself as much as possible from bright computer screens in the evening hours, an artificial daylight is standing by in my office for the darkest months

prevention.t: Stay connected socially - people easily become lonely if they do not feel part of the group.
prevention.q: We are social beings after all, and we may easily become lonely if we don't feel part of the group

prevention.t: Going to the gym helped an ESA doctor out of a low "semi-hibernation" mood.
prevention.q: To get out of my dark mood of semi-hibernation I tried to motivate myself to go to the gym.

summary.t: Spaceflight brings work overload, irregular light-dark cycles and disrupted sleep patterns.
summary.q: Astronauts are exposed to numerous stressors during spaceflight, such as work overload, irregular light-dark cycles, and sleep-pattern disruptions.

summary.t: Insomnia means regularly having problems sleeping. It usually improves by changing sleep habits.
summary.q: Insomnia means you regularly have problems sleeping. It usually gets better by changing your sleeping habits.

redflag.t: Seven days of six-hour nights leaves performance as poor as staying awake 24-36 hours straight.
redflag.q: after seven days of six hours of sleep, a person's performance is equal to that of a person who has not slept for 24 to 36 consecutive hours.

symptom.t: Lack of sleep slows thinking and harms reasoning and memory.
symptom.q: Lack of sleep slows mental processes and compromises reasoning ability and memory

symptom.t: Hard to fall asleep, waking several times, or waking early and not getting back to sleep.
symptom.q: find it hard to go to sleep wake up several times during the night lie awake at night wake up early and cannot go back to sleep

symptom.t: Still tired after waking; tired and irritable during the day.
symptom.q: still feel tired after waking up ... feel tired and irritable during the day

risk.t: The ISS sees 16 sunrises and sunsets a day, which can disrupt the sleep-wake cycle.
risk.q: Astronauts witness 16 sunrises and sunsets per day aboard the space station, which can disrupt their sleep-wake cycle.

risk.t: Sleep loss, body-clock disruption and work overload add to the stress of isolation.
risk.q: Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload compound this issue and may lead to decreased performance, adverse health outcomes, and compromised mission objectives.

risk.t: Common causes: stress, anxiety or depression.
risk.q: The most common causes of insomnia are: ... stress, anxiety or depression

risk.t: Noise, a room that is too hot or cold, uncomfortable beds.
risk.q: noise ... a room that's too hot or cold ... uncomfortable beds

prevention.t: ISS LED lighting mimics Earth's day-night cycle to help sleep.
prevention.q: light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, simulate Earth's light-dark cycle to help astronauts sleep better.

prevention.t: Crews get scheduled time to relax and for self-care to prevent burnout.
prevention.q: Astronauts are also given designated times for relaxation and self-care as part of their routine to help prevent burnout.

prevention.t: Keep the sleep space cool, dark and quiet, with no screens.
prevention.q: Ensure a Cool/Dark/Quiet Sleep Space (no TV/computers)

prevention.t: No caffeine for 6-12 hours before sleep.
prevention.q: No caffeine 6-12 hrs prior to sleep (individual dependent)

prevention.t: Get bright light in the 1-2 hours after waking.
prevention.q: 1-2 hrs After Waking: Seek bright light/blue enriched light/high (CCT)

dont.t: Avoid screens right before bed - blue light keeps you awake.
dont.q: do not watch television or use devices, like smartphones, right before going to bed, because the blue light makes you more awake

dont.t: Do not drive when sleepy.
dont.q: do not drive when you feel sleepy

dont.t: No smoking, alcohol, tea or coffee for at least 6 hours before bed.
dont.q: do not smoke or drink alcohol, tea or coffee at least 6 hours before going to bed

escalate.t: See a doctor if changing sleep habits has not helped.
escalate.q: changing your sleeping habits has not helped your insomnia

escalate.t: See a GP if changing habits has not helped.
escalate.q: changing your sleeping habits has not helped your insomnia

escalate.t: See a GP if sleep problems have lasted months.
escalate.q: you've had trouble sleeping for months

differential.t: Snoring or pauses in breathing during sleep (sleep apnoea) can be a cause; a sleep clinic may be needed.
differential.q: snoring or interrupted breathing while sleeping (sleep apnoea)

action.t: Only go to bed when sleepy.
action.q: only go to bed when you're sleepy

action.t: Get up at the same time every day.
action.q: wake up and get out of bed at the same time every day

action.t: Relax for at least 1 hour before bed (e.g. bath or book).
action.q: relax at least 1 hour before bed – for example, take a bath or read a book

action.t: Keep the bedroom dark and quiet; use blinds, eye mask or ear plugs.
action.q: make sure your bedroom is dark and quiet – use curtains, blinds, an eye mask or ear plugs if needed

action.t: Exercise regularly during the day.
action.q: exercise regularly during the day

action.t: Make sure the mattress, pillows and covers are comfortable.
action.q: make sure your mattress, pillows and covers are comfortable

summary.t: Most astronauts get motion sickness in space.
summary.q: The majority of astronauts experience motion sickness during spaceflight.

summary.t: Weightlessness and changes between gravity levels can cause motion sickness and make it hard to tell which way is up.
summary.q: Altered gravity and shifts between different types of gravity may trigger motion sickness and affect astronauts' ability to orient themselves.

symptom.t: The four most common symptoms are nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and an uneasy 'stomach awareness'.
symptom.q: the four most frequently reported symptoms of SMS: nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and stomach awareness.

symptom.t: Other symptoms: looking pale, feeling warm, cold sweats, feeling generally unwell, tiredness.
symptom.q: they include: pallor, increased body warmth, cold sweating, malaise, loss of appetite, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, and anorexia.

symptom.t: Sluggishness, disorientation and poor concentration are also part of space motion sickness.
symptom.q: include malaise, sluggishness, disorientation, ... impaired concentration, stomach awareness, ... decreased appetite, nausea, and vomiting.

redflag.t: Severe case: more than 2 vomiting episodes, clear drop in performance, or symptoms lasting beyond 72 hours.
redflag.q: includes more than 2 episodes of vomiting; significant performance decrement may be apparent; symptoms may persist beyond 72 hours

redflag.t: The main health worries are dehydration and weakness, plus reduced ability to work.
redflag.q: Concerns include health decrements (dehydration and weakness) and decreased crew performance.

dont.t: No spacewalks while symptomatic or before flight day 3 - vomiting inside a spacesuit can be fatal.
dont.q: Currently, EVAs cannot be performed by symptomatic crew or prior to flight day three due to the lack of a consistently efficacious drug, concern about neurocognitive side effects, and because an in-suit vomiting episode is potentially fatal.

action.t: Things that ease symptoms: focusing on a task, closing your eyes, limiting activity and keeping your head still.
action.q: Attenuating Factors ... Concentration on performing a task ... Closing eyes ... Restricting activity ... Restricting head motion

action.t: Non-drug measures: minimise head and provoking movements, increase air flow, keep hydrated.
action.q: Training to minimize head and provocative movements ... Increased air movement/circulation ... Maintain hydration

escalate.t: Whether and how to treat or prevent it is decided with the flight surgeon.
escalate.q: The prevention or treatment of SAS is determined per discretion of crew in coordination with their flight surgeon.

escalate.t: If motion sickness is severe, IV fluids may be considered (crew medical officer / flight surgeon decision).
escalate.q: If SMS or TRMS is severe, consider IV hydration

monitor.t: ISS crew have a private medical conference with the flight surgeon on launch day and daily for 5 days.
monitor.q: crew have daily private medical conferences (PMC) on launch day and daily for 5 days per the NASA Medical Operations Requirements Document (MORD).

risk.t: Getting car or sea sick on Earth does not predict how sick you will get in space.
risk.q: The sickness you experience traveling in cars, boats, and planes on Earth does not predict how motion sick you may get during space travel.

risk.t: It is worse on a first flight, and having had it before predicts having it again.
risk.q: previous SAS experience can predict reoccurrence, SAS is worse in first flyers

risk.t: The cause is a mismatch between what the inner ear and the eyes report, leading to disorientation, tiredness and nausea.
risk.q: This sensory mismatch leads to disorientation, fatigue, and nausea.

meds.name: Promethazine
meds.purpose: Treats space motion sickness symptoms (nausea, vomiting); given by the crew medical officer / flight surgeon from the onboard kit.
meds.q: NASA treatment of choice and most effective in-flight SMS treatment found to date is promethazine.

cautions.t: When someone is vomiting, an injection or suppository may be preferred because tablets may not stay down.
cautions.q: In more severe cases of SMS, IM or PR may be preferred as vomiting can interfere with oral dosing.

cautions.t: On Earth promethazine often causes drowsiness, which could affect operations.
cautions.q: The incidence of sedation associated with promethazine administration on the ground is large and may result in operational impact.

cautions.t: Astronauts who took promethazine had 3 times the odds of urinary retention in flight.
cautions.q: the odds of developing urinary retention in spaceflight is 3 times higher among astronauts who took promethazine.

cautions.t: Anticholinergic motion-sickness medicines can interfere with the bladder and cause urinary retention.
cautions.q: Anticholinergic medications often used to prevent space adaptation sickness can interfere with normal bladder function causing urinary retention.

cautions.t: Each astronaut tests the medicine before flight to check for unusual reactions.
cautions.q: Preflight testing of medication was considered mandatory to test for idiosyncratic reactions and side effects.

summary.t: Long weightlessness shifts fluid to the head, which can swell the optic nerve, fold the retina, flatten the back of the eye and swell the brain - together called SANS.
summary.q: Chronic weightlessness can cause bodily fluids such as blood and cerebrospinal fluid to move toward the head, which can lead to optic nerve swelling, folds in the retina, flattening of the back of the eye, and swelling in the brain.

summary.t: SANS findings: optic disc swelling, flattening of the back of the eyeball, chorioretinal folds and a long-sighted (hyperopic) shift in vision.
summary.q: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) refers to a constellation of ocular findings including optic disc edema, posterior globe flattening, chorioretinal folds, and hyperopic shifts in refractive error observed in astronauts during and following long-duration spaceflight.

symptom.t: About 29% (short missions) and 60% (long missions) of astronauts noticed worse distance and near vision.
symptom.q: approximately 29% and 60% of astronauts on short and long-duration missions, respectively, experienced a degradation in distant and near visual acuity.

symptom.t: A long-sighted shift can cause eye strain and blurred near vision.
symptom.q: hyperopic patients may experience eyestrain and/or blurred near vision

symptom.t: In a study of astronauts after 6-month flights, 6 of 7 had reduced near vision.
symptom.q: decreased near vision in 6 astronauts

risk.t: The risk is higher on longer missions.
risk.q: The risk of developing SANS is higher during longer-duration missions and remains a top research priority for scientists ahead of a Mars mission.

risk.t: Possible risk factors: the weightless environment, diet changes, pockets of CO2, repeat flights.
risk.q: Potential Risk Factors ... Space/microgravity environment ... Nutritional changes ... CO2 air pockets ... Repeat flyers

action.t: Every crewmember flies with at least 3 pairs of prescription glasses of different strengths to correct vision changes.
action.q: All crew fly with at least 3 pairs of prescription lenses of varying power to help compensate for vision decrements in-flight.

action.t: 'Space anticipation glasses' help with long-sighted vision changes in flight.
action.q: Space Anticipation Glasses Used to help crewmembers with inflight vision changes due to hyperopic shifts.

monitor.t: Eyes are checked before, during and after flight.
monitor.q: Crewmembers are monitored pre-flight, inflight, and post-flight for changes and any associated vision decrements.

monitor.t: Astronauts image their own retinas in orbit so doctors can track eye changes.
monitor.q: Using this tool to examine the retina helps scientists track how the spaceflight environment affects the human eye.

escalate.t: Folds that keep getting worse during a mission could permanently harm vision, so new or worsening vision changes need medical review.
escalate.q: Persistent progressive folds during missions can potentially degrade vision and increase risk of debilitating uncorrectable vision defects.

prevention.t: NASA is studying supplements and devices that reverse fluid shift toward the head to prevent SANS.
prevention.q: NASA scientists are investigating potential ways to prevent or treat SANS, including nutritional supplements that could protect the eyes and mechanical interventions that may help reverse headward fluid shifts.

prevention.t: Thigh cuffs may reduce fluid shift toward the head.
prevention.q: Thigh cuffs may reduce fluid shifts and improve venous congestion and ICP changes.

summary.t: Kidney stones in flight are a high-severity risk: the pain affects work and complications (blood in urine, infection, kidney swelling, sepsis) could force evacuation.
summary.q: The formation of renal stones poses an in-flight health risk of high severity, not only because of the impact of renal colic on human performance but also because of complications that could potentially lead to crew evacuation, such as hematuria, infection, hydronephrosis, and sepsis.

symptom.t: A stone in flight could cause colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, blood in urine, infection or a swollen kidney.
symptom.q: possibility that symptomatic renal stones will occur, which could cause renal colic (pain), nausea, vomiting, hematuria, infection, and/or hydronephrosis.

symptom.t: Stone pain usually starts in the side of the tummy or the lower back.
symptom.q: usually starts in the side of your tummy (abdomen) or lower back

symptom.t: The pain may spread to the groin (top of inner thigh), testicles or around the vaginal opening.
symptom.q: may spread to the area at the top of your inner thigh (groin), your testicles or the area around the opening of your vagina

redflag.t: Urgent help if you may have a stone and are in severe pain or have a high temperature / feel hot, cold or shivery (possible infection).
redflag.q: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if: ... you're in severe pain ... you have a high temperature, or you feel hot, cold or shivery

escalate.t: If a stone is suspected in flight, ultrasound and limited lab tests can help detect and manage it (crew medical officer with flight surgeon).
escalate.q: If renal stones are suspected in-flight, ultrasound and limited lab work can detect and help enable stone risk management.

action.t: Most stones are treated at home: drink lots of water; medicines may be offered for pain, sickness and to help pass the stone.
action.q: You'll be advised to drink lots of water and may be offered medicines to help with the symptoms, such as: painkillers ... anti-sickness medicines ... medicines to help the stones come out in your pee

risk.t: Bone loss in weightlessness raises calcium in the blood and urine, raising stone risk.
risk.q: Exposure to microgravity induces bone atrophy/bone loss which increases circulating calcium, impacting the renal stone risk.

risk.t: Drinking less water because of busy schedules and awkward toilet logistics.
risk.q: Decreased water intake (due to busy schedules and time-consuming logistics of urination).

risk.t: Diet high in salt (sodium) and animal protein.
risk.q: Changes in nutrient intake including high sodium and high animal protein.

risk.t: Without prevention, dehydration and calcium lost from bones raise kidney stone risk.
risk.q: If preventive measures are not implemented, crews may experience an increased risk of developing kidney stones due to dehydration and increased excretion of calcium from their bones.

prevention.t: Drink enough water - crews must have plenty available and be encouraged to drink.
prevention.q: Hydration - ensure crew has ample supply of water and is encouraged to drink an adequate amount.

prevention.t: Exercise protects bone and lowers stone-forming calcium in urine.
prevention.q: Exercise can preserve bone mineral density, decreasing the amount of stone forming calcium in urine.

prevention.t: Manage intake of stone-forming substances such as oxalate, calcium, magnesium and salt.
prevention.q: Manage the amount of stone forming substances including oxalate, calcium, magnesium, and salt

prevention.t: Adults: drink 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day (Earth guidance).
prevention.q: drink 2.5 to 3 litres of water each day if you're an adult

prevention.t: Keep salt below 6 g a day (adults).
prevention.q: do not have too much salt in your diet - adults should have less than 6g a day

monitor.t: Check your pee colour - dark pee means you need to drink more.
monitor.q: check the colour of your pee - if your pee is dark, it means you're dehydrated and need to drink more

meds.name: NSAIDs or opioids (pain relief)
meds.purpose: Pain relief for stone pain; choice and use decided by the crew medical officer / flight surgeon.
meds.q: NSAIDS and opioids can assist with stone pain

cautions.t: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen may not be suitable if you have had an allergic reaction to ibuprofen, aspirin or another NSAID.
cautions.q: you've had an allergic reaction to ibuprofen, aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)

cautions.t: May not be suitable with a current or past stomach ulcer.
cautions.q: you have a stomach ulcer or you've had them before

cautions.t: May not be suitable with a heart, liver or kidney condition.
cautions.q: you have a heart, liver or kidney condition

cautions.t: NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen can cause urinary retention.
cautions.q: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as aspirin and ibuprofen

meds.name: Ondansetron
meds.purpose: Anti-sickness medicine for nausea with stone pain (crew medical officer / flight surgeon decision).
meds.q: ondansetron can assist with nausea associated with stone pain.

summary.t: When CO2 builds up in the body (hypercapnia) it can cause headache, breathlessness, tiredness and, in extreme cases, death.
summary.q: CO2 can build-up in our bodies (hypercapnia) and cause symptoms such as headache, dyspnea, fatigue, and in extreme cases, death.

summary.t: Hypoxia means body tissues get less oxygen than normal.
summary.q: a condition that occurs when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal

symptom.t: Typical short-term symptoms: headache, minor vision disturbances and subtle behaviour changes.
symptom.q: Typical acute symptoms include headache, minor visual disturbances, and subtle behavioral changes.

symptom.t: Crews have reported headache, fatigue and malaise at CO2 levels lower than those that cause symptoms on Earth.
symptom.q: Reports of space flight crewmembers becoming symptomatic with headaches, fatigue, and malaise at levels below those known to cause such symptoms terrestrially

symptom.t: Headaches reported at about 2.8-4.5 mmHg CO2.
symptom.q: Headaches at levels between 2.8-4.5 mmHg

redflag.t: Poor CO2 removal can progress from headache and fatigue to impaired thinking and death.
redflag.q: the consequence of inadequate CO2 removal can result in hypercapnia and related symptoms ranging from headache and fatigue to impaired cognitive function and death.

redflag.t: Get medical help immediately: problems with balance or coordination.
redflag.q: have problems with balance or coordination

redflag.t: Get medical help immediately: short of breath even at rest.
redflag.q: feel short of breath, even when resting

redflag.t: Get medical help immediately: coughing up frothy or bloody spit.
redflag.q: have a cough or are coughing up frothy or bloody spit

differential.t: Headache and vision changes in space are also commonly caused by fluid shift toward the head, not only by CO2.
differential.q: These two symptoms are commonly linked to fluid shifts and potential increase in intra-cranial pressure (ICP) due to the microgravity environment in spaceflight.

risk.t: CO2 can pool in one spot without fresh-air flow, so a crewmember rebreathes their own exhaled CO2 - much higher than the module average shows.
risk.q: This results in the crew rebreathing CO2 from their exhaled breath, exposing them to a much higher concentration of CO2 than whole-module measurements would suggest.

risk.t: Pockets of CO2 form where gas is produced without a way to purge the area with fresh air.
risk.q: One is the problem of pockets of CO2 in the habitat caused by excess generation of the gas in one location without a mechanism to purge the area with fresh air.

risk.t: Some individuals seem more sensitive to CO2 than others.
risk.q: anecdotal reports from the International Space Station (ISS) crews suggest that certain individuals may experience a greater susceptibility.

risk.t: During spacewalks CO2 builds up from breathing inside the small closed suit.
risk.q: When astronauts go on a Spacewalk/EVA (extravehicular activity), they build up CO2 levels from breathing into a small closed space.

prevention.t: Sleeping areas need good ventilation to stop CO2 building up around the head.
prevention.q: Adequate ventilation of the sleeping area is required to preclude unacceptable carbon dioxide levels and odors in head positions.

prevention.t: NASA's standard limits the 1-hour average cabin CO2 to 3 mmHg.
prevention.q: The system shall limit the average one-hour CO2 partial pressure (ppCO2) in the habitable volume to no more than 3 mmHg.

prevention.t: Drink enough water so you do not get dehydrated (Earth altitude advice).
prevention.q: drink enough water so you do not get dehydrated

meds.name: Analgesics (acetaminophen/paracetamol, aspirin or NSAIDs) for headache
meds.purpose: Headache relief in space (NASA lists these for space-adaptation headache); CO2 itself still needs to be lowered.
meds.q: Treatment includes sleep, exercise, hydration, coffee intake, and analgesics including acetaminophen, aspirin, or NSAIDS.

cautions.t: Ibuprofen/NSAIDs may not be suitable after an allergic reaction to ibuprofen, aspirin or another NSAID.
cautions.q: you've had an allergic reaction to ibuprofen, aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)

cautions.t: Ibuprofen may not be suitable with asthma or allergies.
cautions.q: you have asthma or allergies (such as hay fever)

cautions.t: Ibuprofen may not be suitable with a current or past stomach ulcer.
cautions.q: you have a stomach ulcer or you've had them before

cautions.t: Do not take ibuprofen together with other NSAIDs such as aspirin.
cautions.q: Do not take ibuprofen at the same time as other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as naproxen or aspirin.

action.t: Tell the people you are with that you feel unwell (Earth altitude-sickness advice).
action.q: tell someone who you're travelling with that you do not feel well

summary.t: In decompression sickness ('the bends'), nitrogen dissolved in the blood forms bubbles that can damage tissues.
summary.q: During decompression sickness, dissolved nitrogen in the bloodstream begins to bubble, which can damage body tissues.

risk.t: In space it can happen when moving from the spacecraft into a lower-pressure spacesuit for a spacewalk.
risk.q: In space, this same phenomenon can occur when an astronaut moves from a spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit for spacewalks.

risk.t: Going from higher to lower pressure too fast without enough nitrogen wash-out causes DCS; it is also a concern if the cabin depressurises.
risk.q: Moving from a higher to a lower pressure too quickly and without adequate denitrogenation can cause decompression sickness (DCS).

risk.t: Cabin depressurisation is another situation where DCS must be minimised.
risk.q: DCS should also be minimized during off-nominal events such as cabin depressurization.

risk.t: Susceptibility factors include a patent foramen ovale (PFO), body fat %, hydration and exercise type.
risk.q: Several factors can increase an individual's susceptibility to DCS, including the presence of a patent foramen ovale (PFO), body fat %, hydration, and exercise type.

symptom.t: The bubbles can cause pain severe enough to make a diver double over.
symptom.q: nitrogen gas dissolved in their body tissues rapidly forms bubbles which can cause pain so severe it may force a diver to double over.

symptom.t: Most common signs: joint pain and numbness or tingling.
symptom.q: The most common manifestations of DCS are joint pain and numbness or tingling.

symptom.t: Next most common: muscle weakness and being unable to empty a full bladder.
symptom.q: The next most common are muscular weakness and inability to empty a full bladder.

redflag.t: Severe cases: bubbles can affect breathing or block blood vessels and cause stroke-like symptoms.
redflag.q: In severe cases, these bubbles can impact breathing or even block blood vessels and cause stroke-like symptoms.

redflag.t: Emergency: profound dizziness, trouble breathing, altered consciousness, abnormal walking or weakness.
redflag.q: The diver may be profoundly dizzy or have trouble breathing. Neurological symptoms may manifest as altered consciousness, abnormal gait or weakness.

redflag.t: Numbness, tingling and/or paralysis; shortness of breath.
redflag.q: Numbness, tingling and/or paralysis Shortness of breath

redflag.t: Confusion, personality change or odd behaviour; collapse or unconsciousness.
redflag.q: Confusion, personality changes or bizarre behavior ... Unconsciousness or collapse

action.t: If DCS symptoms start during a spacewalk, safely but quickly end it and return to the pressurised spacecraft.
action.q: Current protocols hold that when experiencing decompression sickness symptoms, astronauts should safely but rapidly end their spacewalk and return to the pressurized environment of their spacecraft.

action.t: There is no hyperbaric chamber in space, but crew with DCS symptoms can get a treatment similar in principle (raising suit/cabin pressure).
action.q: While a hyperbaric chamber is not available during spaceflight, crewmembers exhibiting DCS symptoms may undergo a treatment similar in principle to the Navy table treatments.

action.t: Early oxygen first aid is essential and may reduce symptoms.
action.q: Early oxygen first aid is essential and may reduce symptoms, but this should not change the treatment plan.

escalate.t: Always get a doctor trained in this to assess suspected DCS, even if symptoms seem to have gone.
escalate.q: Always contact DAN or a physician trained in dive medicine in cases of suspected decompression illness - even if the signs and symptoms appear resolved.

escalate.t: Delays raise the risk of lasting damage.
escalate.q: Delays in seeking treatment elevate the risk of residual symptoms.

dont.t: Do not treat the pain with painkillers until medical staff say so.
dont.q: Do not attempt to treat the pain with analgesics until advised to do so by medical personnel.

monitor.t: In divers, symptoms usually appear from 15 minutes up to 12 hours after surfacing (diving data).
monitor.q: Signs and symptoms usually appear within 15 minutes or up to 12 hours after surfacing.

prevention.t: Before spacewalks, crews breathe high oxygen ('prebreathe') to wash nitrogen out of the body.
prevention.q: Science-backed protocols prior to spacewalks that involve breathing carefully calibrated high levels of oxygen to displace the nitrogen in the body will also help prevent nitrogen bubbles from forming when traveling to a lower-pressure environment.

prevention.t: Prebreathe protocols expose crew to high oxygen before spacewalks to remove nitrogen and lower DCS risk.
prevention.q: to ensure crew members are exposed to high levels of oxygen before spacewalks, primarily to help remove nitrogen from the body and mitigate the risk of decompression sickness.

summary.t: Astronauts often get back pain in flight, probably because the spine lengthens without gravity.
summary.q: Astronauts have complained of back pain occurring during spaceflight, presumably due to the elongation of the spine from the lack of gravity.

symptom.t: It usually appears in the first 2-5 days of flight.
symptom.q: Space Adaptation Back Pain (SABP) occurs in 52% of space travelers during the first 2-5 days of flight.

symptom.t: Most cases are mild (86%); 11% moderate, 3% severe.
symptom.q: Most of the affected astronauts reported mild pain (86%). Moderate pain was reported by 11% of the affected astronauts and severe pain was reported by 3% of the affected astronauts.

risk.t: In space the spine straightens and lengthens; height can increase by up to 3%.
risk.q: the spines of astronauts will straighten out and elongate in space. Consequently, the height of crew members can increase as much as 3% in space.

risk.t: Losing the normal back curve can cause pain and reduce spine stability.
risk.q: Microgravity reduces the usual back curve causing it to straighten, potentially causing pain and degrading spine stability.

risk.t: Astronauts have 4.3 times the rate of herniated (slipped) discs compared with matched non-flyers.
risk.q: The incidence of HNP was 4.3 times higher in the U.S. astronaut population (N=321) compared to matched controls (N=983) not involved in spaceflight.

risk.t: The disc herniation risk is highest right after returning from space.
risk.q: Astronauts are at higher risk of incurring HNP, especially immediately following spaceflight.

action.t: Most effective in-flight treatments: curling into a fetal position (91%), plus painkillers and exercise such as treadmill or cycling (85%).
action.q: The most effective treatments were fetal positioning (91%) and the use of analgesic medications and exercise (primarily treadmill and cycle ergometer), which were both 85% effective.

action.t: Stay active and keep doing daily activities.
action.q: stay active and try to continue with your daily activities

action.t: A wrapped heat pack can ease stiffness or muscle spasms.
action.q: use a heat pack (or hot water bottle) wrapped in a tea towel to relieve joint stiffness or muscle spasms

action.t: Try back exercises and stretches - stop if the pain gets worse.
action.q: There are specific exercises and stretches you can do to help with back pain. But stop if your pain gets worse and see a GP for advice.

dont.t: Do not stay in bed for long periods.
dont.q: do not stay in bed for long periods of time

redflag.t: Emergency (999): pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs.
redflag.q: pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs

redflag.t: Emergency (999): loss of feeling around the genitals or anus.
redflag.q: a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus

redflag.t: Emergency (999): bladder or bowel changes, such as difficulty peeing or wetting/soiling yourself.
redflag.q: changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself

redflag.t: Emergency (999): back pain with chest pain, or after a serious accident.
redflag.q: chest pain ... it started after a serious accident, such as a car accident

escalate.t: Urgent: back pain with feeling hot, cold, shivery or unwell, or severe pain that starts suddenly or worsens quickly.
escalate.q: you feel hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell ... it's severe pain that starts suddenly, or it's getting worse quickly

monitor.t: See a doctor if it has not improved after a few weeks of home treatment, is worse at night, or is worse when sneezing/coughing.
monitor.q: it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks ... it does not improve after resting or is worse at night ... it's worse when sneezing, coughing or pooing

cautions.q: check with a pharmacist or GP if you're unsure about which painkiller is suitable for you

summary.t: Long isolation and confinement can increase behavioural problems and psychiatric disorders such as anxiety and depression.
summary.q: The prolonged isolation and confinement that astronauts face in space can increase risks of behavioral issues and psychiatric disorders, such as anxiety and depression.

summary.t: Common concerns in spaceflight include stress, depression, anxiety, relationship problems and grief.
summary.q: Common behavioral health conditions or concerns in the spaceflight environment may include stress, depression, anxiety, relationship problems, and grief.

risk.t: The longer the mission, the higher the chance of these problems.
risk.q: Anecdotal and empirical evidence indicate that the likelihood of an adverse cognitive or behavioral condition or psychiatric disorder occurring greatly increases with the length of a mission.

risk.t: Sleep loss, body-clock disruption and overwork make isolation harder.
risk.q: Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload compound this issue and may lead to decreased performance, adverse health outcomes, and compromised mission objectives.

risk.t: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth and other stresses can all affect mental health.
risk.q: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth, and other intense space stressors may all take a toll on the mental health of the crew.

symptom.t: Low mood can make you feel sad, anxious or panicky, angry or frustrated, and low in confidence.
symptom.q: A general low mood can make you feel sad, anxious or panicky, angry or frustrated and low on confidence and self-esteem.

symptom.t: Low mood can also cause tiredness or sleep problems.
symptom.q: It can also make you feel tired, or cause problems sleeping.

symptom.t: Feeling irritable and intolerant of others.
symptom.q: feeling irritable and intolerant of others

redflag.t: Suicidal thoughts or thoughts of self-harm are a warning sign of depression.
redflag.q: having suicidal thoughts or thoughts about harming yourself

redflag.t: If someone has seriously harmed themselves or may be about to, it is an emergency (NHS: call 999).
redflag.q: If you have seriously harmed yourself - for example, by taking a drug overdose - or you feel that you may be about to harm yourself, call 999 for an ambulance or go straight to A&E.

escalate.t: Get medical help if low mood lasts more than 2 weeks or you are struggling to cope.
escalate.q: you've had a low mood for more than 2 weeks you're struggling to cope with a low mood

action.t: Talk about your feelings with a friend, family member or health professional.
action.q: try talking about your feelings to a friend, family member, healthcare professional or counsellor

action.t: ISS crew can talk virtually with family and medical professionals for support.
action.q: Crew members aboard the International Space Station can virtually talk with family and medical professionals for support

action.t: Private psychological conferences with the ground are provided, plus care packages and other support.
action.q: Private psychological conferences (PPCs) are currently provided

prevention.t: NASA encourages self-care such as keeping a regular journal.
prevention.q: To improve mental health, NASA encourages astronauts to explore self-care options including keeping a regular journal.

prevention.t: Growing fresh vegetables may help as a reminder of life on Earth.
prevention.q: research suggests growing fresh vegetables in space may provide therapeutic benefits by providing a tangible reminder of life back on Earth.

prevention.t: Looking out of windows reduces monotony and the feeling of confinement.
prevention.q: A spacecraft's windows can boost the mental health of astronauts because they reduce monotony and the sense of confinement while in space.

prevention.t: Regular exercise may improve mood and sleep.
prevention.q: get regular exercise - this may improve your mood and help you sleep better

prevention.t: Learn to relax with calming breathing exercises, yoga or pilates.
prevention.q: learn how to relax using calming breathing exercises or try activities such as yoga or pilates

dont.t: Avoid lots of caffeine - it disrupts sleep and makes anxiety harder to control.
dont.q: do not drink lots of coffee, tea, cola or energy drinks - they contain caffeine which can disrupt your sleep and make it harder to control your anxiety
